label: Afternoon edition
summary: Keanu, **Democrats now hold both chambers of Congress**, with NBC projecting about 255 House seats, and Jeffries is naming health care, tariffs and the Iran war as first targets (NBC News, NPR, The Hill). Massie says he will **force a Hegseth impeachment vote Monday**, though CNN's GOP sources expect it to pass while Fox News says most Republicans will oppose it (CNN, Fox News, Washington Examiner). Mississippi's Senate race is still uncalled, with Democrat Scott Colom up about 2,500 votes in CNN's count and mail ballots due Tuesday (CNN, The Hill). In California, Newsom's commutation of all 548 death sentences drew pushback from prosecutors, and **Bay Area voters approved the regional transit tax** that mostly funds BART in Alameda County (SF Chronicle, KQED, Fox News, SF Standard). The Nasdaq bounced 1.09% after Thursday's 5.52% rout, the S&P 500 rose 0.31% and the Dow fell 0.46%, as investors weighed what the midterms mean for AI data centers (CNBC, Fox Business). October payrolls rose 165,000 and unemployment fell to 4.1%, but wages still trail inflation and **a December Fed hike is not a lock** (CNBC, Axios, Fox Business). In Ukraine, a Russian strike on an aid center killed at least 53 ahead of talks in Abu Dhabi Nov. 10-11 (CNN, Axios). Texas's grid queue holds **474 GW of data center requests**, and Sanders is calling for a national moratorium (Axios, CNBC). Anthropic's revised S-1 shows $17 billion in Q3 revenue and $895.4 billion in commitments (CNBC, Bloomberg), and NASA's Swift telescope re-entered over Indonesia after a failed rescue (NASA, Space.com). Fremont looks mild this weekend, with highs in the low 70s and almost no rain.

Nasdaq rebounds 1.09% after its worst day in 18 months, with chips leading.
Newsom commuted 548 death sentences; about 400 need California Supreme Court approval.

Chips led the bounce, with the semiconductor index up about 4.2%, Nvidia up 2.78% and Tesla up 4.23% after Thursday's rout. The strong jobs report raised the odds of a December Fed hike, and the 10-year yield sat at 4.86% (CNBC, Axios). CoreWeave's 2032 bond yield topped 16% in a sign of **AI credit stress** (CNBC).

stories.title: Democrats win both chambers and set an agenda of health care, tariffs and ending the Iran war
stories.summary: NBC projects about 255 House seats for Democrats, and Jeffries names four priorities while Trump promises vetoes.
story: Democrats won control of both chambers of Congress in Tuesday's midterms, NBC News and The Hill reported. NBC projects about 255 House seats, well above the 218 needed, and Alaska and Mississippi Senate results were still pending as of Friday. Hakeem Jeffries is expected to become speaker when the new Congress convenes Jan. 3, and Chuck Schumer is expected to return as Senate majority leader after leadership elections in early December (NBC News, NPR, The Hill).

NPR reports that the first 100 hours would target restoring enhanced Affordable Care Act subsidies and reversing Medicaid cuts. Jeffries has also named reasserting Congress's authority over tariffs and stopping the Iran war. In the Senate, most bills still need 60 votes. NBC notes that Mike Johnson may not stay as the top House Republican, though NBC says no decision from him has been confirmed.

Trump has swung between promising to be 'Mr. Veto' and saying he hopes to work with Democrats, NPR and The Hill report. Overriding a veto takes two-thirds of both chambers, which Democrats lack. Fox News reports Republicans are already fighting over blame, with Vance, Cruz and DeSantis giving different diagnoses. NPR adds that the party remains unpopular and divided between those who want sweeping change and those who favor gradual steps.

Democrats will gain subpoena power, so oversight of the Iran war, tariffs and cabinet officials is likely to dominate 2027. Republicans may try to pass a party-line reconciliation bill and a debt ceiling increase in the lame-duck session first.
facts: NBC News projects Democrats will win about 255 House seats.
Jeffries is expected to be sworn in as speaker on Jan. 3 (NBC News).
Schumer is expected to be elected majority leader in early December (NPR).
Democrats' first priorities are ACA subsidies, Medicaid cuts, tariff authority and the Iran war (NPR).
Trump can veto any bill, and Democrats lack a two-thirds majority (NPR, The Hill).
stories.left: Voters ran on affordability and rejected tariffs, Medicaid cuts and an unauthorized war. Democrats say the mandate is to restore health coverage, check a president who ignored Congress, and use subpoena power to investigate. They argue that vetoes will show Trump choosing his policies over voters' costs.
stories.right: Democrats won on cost-of-living anger, not on a mandate for their full agenda, and polls still show the party unpopular. Conservatives warn that investigations, a data center moratorium and repealing tariffs would raise costs and weaken America against China. Thune says Republicans will work to stop the worst impulses of Democratic extremism.
stories.next: The lame-duck House returns Monday Nov. 9; Senate Democrats hold leadership elections in early December and the new Congress starts Jan. 3.

stories.title: Vance blames the Iran war for the Republican rout, while Toomey, Cruz and conservative writers cite tariffs
stories.summary: Trump partly agrees with Vance's war diagnosis, and right-leaning outlets split over tariffs, the war and Trump's treatment of Congress.
story: JD Vance wrote that 'the reason we lost is the war,' naming frustration over the war, rising costs and ties with Israel as reasons 2024 Trump voters defected, Fox News reported. Trump gave a mixed answer. He said 'I don't think it's the war, Bret, I think it's the gasoline price,' while also saying the war likely contributed (Fox News). A White House official said the results 'would have looked very different without the Iran War.'

Other Republicans pointed elsewhere. Former Sen. Pat Toomey called Vance 'mistaken' to blame only the war and said arbitrary tariffs raised costs for consumers, per Fox News. Sen. Ted Cruz said tariffs made everything too expensive and the war dragged on too long. The Dispatch argued tariffs were a millstone for the party, and The Dispatch's piece says the war was not what caused the blue wave.

National Review argued that Trump lost the congressional GOP by treating it with contempt over tariffs, the war, cabinet appointments and immigration enforcement. Another National Review piece said Trump's corruption scandals deepened the losses. Fox News reports the fight is also a preview of a 2028 showdown, with Vance trying to separate himself from Trump on foreign policy.
The argument matters because it will shape what Republicans do in the lame-duck session and which issues they carry into 2028.
facts: Vance wrote 'The reason we lost is the war' (Fox News).
Trump said he thought it was the gasoline price and that the war likely contributed (Fox News).
Toomey and Cruz cited tariffs as a major cost driver (Fox News).
The Dispatch and National Review blame tariffs and Trump's handling of Congress.
Trump has said he will keep Hegseth (Fox News).
stories.left: Republicans are only now admitting what voters said: the war and tariffs raised prices, and the president ignored Congress and the public. Democrats say the blame game does not undo the damage. They want oversight of how decisions were made, and an end to the war and the tariffs.
stories.right: The loss has several causes, and conservative writers disagree sharply about which mattered most. Some argue tariffs and Trump's contempt for congressional allies did the damage, as National Review and The Dispatch say. Others say the real failure was an unfinished fight with a nuclear-seeking Iran, and that blaming the war lets the party dodge harder questions about its economic message.
stories.next: Watch the lame-duck House starting Nov. 9 and whether Trump moves on Hegseth or on tariffs.

stories.title: Massie says he will force a Hegseth impeachment vote when the House returns Nov. 9
stories.summary: Reports differ on whether the House would impeach, with GOP sources telling CNN it could pass and Fox saying most Republicans oppose it.
story: Rep. Thomas Massie, a Kentucky Republican, told CNN he plans to force a vote to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth when the House returns Monday, Nov. 9, and multiple GOP sources told CNN they expect it to pass. The Washington Examiner reports Massie offered Hegseth an ultimatum: resign, or face impeachment before the 119th Congress ends. His resolution has eight articles, covering the Iran war, the arrest of Venezuela's Nicolas Maduro, strikes on alleged drug boats and the war in Yemen.

The House's September attempt was stalled when GOP leaders sent members home early, CNN, NBC News and The Hill reported. Speaker Mike Johnson called the effort a publicity stunt and has said the measure would be tabled. Trump has said he has 'every intention to keep' Hegseth and that he is doing a very good job (Fox News, CNN).

Fox News reports that most House Republicans would still vote against impeachment and that one GOP lawmaker doubted it would happen at all. Retiring Rep. Don Bacon has not decided, though he leans against, per the same reports. Massie cites an Economist/YouGov poll with 51% of registered voters supporting impeachment and 34% opposed (Washington Examiner).
Even if the House impeaches, removal needs a Senate trial. With a narrow majority, absences could decide the outcome.
stories.flag: Whether the vote passes is disputed: CNN's GOP sources expect passage, while Fox News reports most Republicans will oppose it.
facts: The House returns Monday, Nov. 9 (CNN, Washington Examiner).
Massie's resolution has eight articles of impeachment (Washington Examiner).
Johnson called it a publicity stunt and has said it would be tabled (Washington Examiner, CNN).
Trump has said he intends to keep Hegseth (CNN, Fox News).
Removal would require a Senate trial (Fox News).
stories.left: Democrats argue Hegseth ran a war without congressional authorization and that Republicans now concede it. They say impeachment is the proper check when a cabinet officer abuses office, and some Republicans agree. The polling majority for impeachment adds to their case.
stories.right: Conservatives say impeachment over policy disagreement abuses the process and the war was a lawful use of the president's power. Johnson calls it a stunt, and Republicans worry about a lame-duck fight that divides the party. Some on the right criticize Hegseth too, but they want Trump, not the House, to decide.
stories.next: The House returns Monday Nov. 9; watch attendance and whether Johnson moves to table.

stories.title: Mississippi's Senate race stays too close to call as provisional and late mail ballots are counted
stories.summary: Democrat Scott Colom leads Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith by roughly 2,500 votes in CNN's count, with provisional ballots and lawyers on both sides.
story: Democrat Scott Colom led Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith by about 2,500 votes with an estimated 97% of the vote counted, CNN reported Friday. Earlier counts were smaller: The Hill put the lead near 1,800 earlier this week, and Fox News carried an even earlier tally of 43 votes. The race is uncalled, and the margins differ because outlets reported at different points in the count.

Mississippi counts mail ballots postmarked by Election Day that arrive within five business days, which runs through Nov. 10. The Hill reports the state's top election official is waiting to see whether about 3,600 outstanding mail ballots arrive. Colom's campaign says about 15,000 provisional ballots await verification (CNN). Hinds County, the largest, planned to work over the weekend.

The state has no automatic recount and no process for a candidate to request one, The Hill reports. The NRSC demanded county officials preserve affidavit ballots, and Colom's campaign called that a desperate stunt (The Hill). Marc Elias's firm says it is leading the legal effort for Colom, and Colom has said he has an army of lawyers (Fox News). The Washington Examiner notes Republicans are relying on late-arriving ballots they asked the Supreme Court to bar this year.
CNN reports the county certification deadline is next Friday. Alaska's Senate race is also still pending.
stories.flag: The final margin is unsettled and could change as provisional and late mail ballots are verified; outlets report different margins from different times.
facts: Colom led by about 2,500 votes with about 97% counted (CNN, Nov. 6).
Mail ballots postmarked by Election Day count if received by Nov. 10 (The Hill).
Mississippi has no automatic recount procedure (The Hill).
Colom's campaign cites about 15,000 provisional ballots (CNN).
County certification is due next Friday (CNN).
stories.left: Every legitimate ballot should be counted, and rules that allow mail ballots postmarked on time were upheld by the Supreme Court. Democrats say the NRSC's demand is an attempt to create doubt about a count that is going their way. A Colom win would show the party competing in deep-red states.
stories.right: Republicans say affidavit and provisional ballots deserve careful scrutiny and that preserving them is ordinary caution in a razor-thin race. The Washington Examiner notes the party had opposed the late-arrival rule on principle. Conservatives also point out that Hyde-Smith has not conceded or been declared the loser, and that the count should finish before conclusions are drawn.
stories.next: Mail ballots are due Tuesday Nov. 10, and counties certify by Friday Nov. 13.

stories.title: Newsom commutes all 548 California death sentences, and prosecutors and victims' families push back
stories.summary: Nearly 400 commutations need California Supreme Court approval, and a legal group has pledged to challenge them.
story: Gov. Gavin Newsom announced Nov. 5 that he is commuting all 548 California death sentences to life without parole, covering 529 men and 19 women, according to SF Chronicle, KQED and CalMatters. If approved, it would be the largest mass commutation of death sentences in U.S. history. In an open letter he called state-sanctioned killing incompatible with California's values and said clemency does not repeal the death penalty.

Because California governors need the state Supreme Court's approval to commute the sentence of anyone twice convicted of a felony, about 400 of the cases need the signatures of four of seven justices, CalMatters reports. In 2018 the court rejected ten Jerry Brown clemency requests without explanation. Anne Marie Schubert of the Criminal Justice Legal Foundation pledged to challenge the commutations in that court.

Fox News reports sharp objections from prosecutors and victims' families. Marc Klaas, whose daughter Polly was murdered in 1993, called it a gift to killers. Orange County DA Todd Spitzer said the move showed mercy for the wolves. Orange County Sheriff Don Barnes noted voters rejected abolition in 2016. LA County DA Nathan Hochman and others noted the action does not eliminate the death penalty. Anti-death-penalty advocates praised the decision.
California has not executed anyone since 2006. Newsom leaves office in January and is widely expected to run for president.
facts: The commutations cover 529 men and 19 women (KQED, SF Chronicle).
About 400 need California Supreme Court approval (CalMatters).
California has not executed anyone since 2006 (KQED).
Voters rejected abolishing the death penalty in 2016 (Fox News).
The Criminal Justice Legal Foundation says it will challenge in court (CalMatters).
stories.left: The death penalty is applied unevenly and risks executing innocent people, and California has not carried out an execution in twenty years. Supporters say commutation to life without parole keeps dangerous people locked up while ending a costly and broken system. They call it moral leadership.
stories.right: Voters kept the death penalty in 2016, and one governor should not erase the verdicts of juries and the wishes of victims' families. Prosecutors say families were not notified in advance. Critics also see a politician acting for his national ambitions in his final months.
stories.next: Watch for a filing at the California Supreme Court from the Criminal Justice Legal Foundation and the court's timeline for the 400 reviews.

stories.title: Bay Area voters approve the regional transit tax, with BART getting most of Alameda County's share
stories.summary: The 14-year sales tax passed with about 62% in early returns and aims to avert BART and Caltrain service cuts.
story: Voters in five Bay Area counties approved the Regional Transit Measure on Nov. 3, SF Standard, KQED and the SF Chronicle reported. Early returns showed about 61.9% yes, and San Francisco's Prop. H, a Muni parcel tax, passed with about 73.6% in early returns. The tax is a half-cent sales tax in Alameda, Contra Costa, San Mateo and Santa Clara counties and one cent in San Francisco, running 14 years.

For Fremont and Alameda County, the measure matters directly. SF Chronicle reports BART would receive nearly 65% of Alameda County's share. Estimates put revenue near $1 billion a year, and the agencies had warned of deep cuts without it. KQED's coverage says the vote averted a transit 'death spiral,' after BART and Caltrain warned of severe service cuts.

The measure requires agencies to adopt cost-cutting plans to get funding, SF Standard reports. A critic noted it says nothing about what happens when the tax expires after 14 years. Totals could shift as the count finishes.
For Keanu, this is the outcome that keeps current BART service running through the next decade.
facts: The measure is a half-cent sales tax (one cent in San Francisco) for 14 years.
Early returns showed about 61.9% yes (SF Chronicle).
BART gets nearly 65% of Alameda County's share (SF Chronicle).
Prop. H passed in San Francisco with about 73.6% in early returns.
The measure does not say what happens after 14 years (SF Standard).
stories.left: Public transit is essential infrastructure, and a sales tax keeps service for workers who cannot drive. Supporters say the cuts would have pushed riders onto already crowded roads, with Bay Bridge delays doubling, per a KQED-reported study. They see the vote as proof that voters will pay for service when agencies show savings.
stories.right: A regional sales tax falls hardest on lower-income shoppers, and agencies should have fixed costs before asking for money. Opponents said transit did not deserve more funding, and a critic notes no plan exists once the tax ends. Conservatives want audits and performance requirements tied to the money.
stories.next: Totals will be certified in the coming weeks; watch BART's first spending plan for Alameda County.

stories.title: Russian bomb strike on a Ukrainian aid center kills 53 as US-Russia-Ukraine talks near
stories.summary: Peace talks open in Abu Dhabi Nov. 10-11 while Trump teases a broad European security deal that Zelensky calls potentially dangerous.
story: Local authorities reported 53 confirmed dead on Friday after Russian guided bombs destroyed a school-turned-aid-distribution center in Komyshuvakha, in Ukraine's Zaporizhzhia region, CNN reported. Many people remained unaccounted for. Earlier counts were lower: AP reported 37 confirmed deaths Tuesday and Zelensky said 43 by Thursday. Officials said victims were in a new EU-funded reinforced basement that collapsed, and the OSCE mission head said the attack appears to violate international humanitarian law.

US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner will lead the American delegation at trilateral talks with Russia and Ukraine in Abu Dhabi on Nov. 10-11, Axios, The Hill and Fox News reported. The agenda covers post-war security arrangements, de-escalation and humanitarian steps. Prospects look weak because the sides remain far apart on territory and Putin has refused a ceasefire.

On Thursday Trump met Kirill Dmitriev, the sanctioned head of Russia's wealth fund and a Putin envoy, then teased a 'big, beautiful' European security agreement without details, CNN reported. Zelensky said it 'can be dangerous' and that ending the war must come before security guarantees. Several European officials told CNN they did not know what Trump meant.
Zelensky has also said Ukraine will keep striking Russian energy targets unless the US delivers more Patriot missiles (Fox News, The Hill).
facts: 53 people were confirmed killed at Komyshuvakha, per local authorities (CNN).
Talks are set for Nov. 10-11 in Abu Dhabi with Witkoff and Kushner (Axios).
Trump met Putin envoy Kirill Dmitriev on Thursday (CNN).
Zelensky said the European security idea 'can be dangerous' (CNN).
The OSCE mission head said the attack appears to violate humanitarian law (CNN).
stories.left: Russia is killing civilians at aid sites while Trump hosts a sanctioned Kremlin envoy, and Democrats say that rewards aggression. They want more air defense for Ukraine and sanctions kept in place. Democrats see the unclear European plan as a sign of a transactional approach that cuts out allies.
stories.right: Conservatives split. Hawks want more Patriots and tougher penalties for Moscow, while others back Trump's push for talks and say Europe should carry more of its own security burden. Supporters of Trump's approach argue that negotiating with Russia, however unpleasant, is the only route to ending the killing.
stories.next: US-Russia-Ukraine talks open in Abu Dhabi Monday Nov. 10; watch for any ceasefire language.

stories.title: Oil swings on Iran diplomacy and tanker attacks as Democrats vow to end the war
stories.summary: Brent fell about 14% early in the week, then rebounded to $98.29 Thursday, and Eurasia Group put the odds of renewed US strikes at 60%.
story: Brent crude fell 8.7% Wednesday to $94.62 after senior US and Iranian officials signaled openness to a diplomatic settlement, CNBC reported, then rose 3.8% Thursday to $98.29 on new tanker attacks. Oil futures were down more than 14% for the week before the rebound. Eurasia Group cut its odds of renewed US strikes on Iran to 60% from 65% and cut the chance of a deal to 10% from 20% (CNBC). WTI traded near $90 Friday.

Trump threatened to 'finish the job' if Iran rejects a nuclear deal, and Iran's Revolutionary Guard vowed united resistance, Fox News reported. Trump also said 'Iran can't have a nuclear weapon' whether or not the war hurt Republicans at the polls.

Democrats say they will try to end the war after January. Schumer said 'We are going to end the war,' and Jeffries pointed to a war powers resolution, NPR reported. NPR notes Democrats lack a veto-proof majority, and a summer Senate vote to end the war failed 47-49. Congress could also limit funds in spending bills.
The Hill's opinion pages argue Tehran has read the election wrong if it thinks time is on its side.
facts: Brent fell 8.7% to $94.62 Wednesday and rose 3.8% to $98.29 Thursday (CNBC).
Eurasia Group put renewed US strike odds at 60% and deal odds at 10% (CNBC).
A summer Senate war powers vote failed 47-49 (NPR).
Democrats cannot override a veto alone (NPR).
Trump said he would finish the job if Iran rejects a nuclear deal (Fox News).
stories.left: The war raised gas prices, was never authorized, and voters said so. Democrats want Congress to reclaim war powers and cut off funds if needed. They argue diplomacy, not escalation, is the way to reopen Hormuz.
stories.right: Iran cannot be allowed a nuclear weapon, and Trump's pressure is what brought Tehran to the table. Conservatives warn that a Democratic push to end the war would hand Iran a victory and encourage attacks on shipping. Others on the right want an exit and criticize the lack of a clear plan.
stories.next: Watch tanker traffic in Hormuz and whether talks with Iran resume before the lame-duck House returns Nov. 9.

stories.title: October jobs beat forecasts, but wages trail inflation and a December Fed hike is not a lock
stories.summary: Payrolls rose 165,000 and unemployment fell to 4.1%, while wage growth of 3.1% lags inflation.
story: US employers added 165,000 jobs in October and unemployment fell to 4.1% from 4.2%, CNBC, Fox Business and Axios reported. Economists polled by LSEG expected about 65,000, per Fox Business. Private payrolls grew 159,000 and average hourly earnings rose 3.1% from a year earlier, above the 2.4% LSEG economists predicted.

The Washington Examiner argues the details were even stronger than the headline, and Axios called it a 'strong hire, low fire' market. Navy Federal's Heather Long said wages are still well below inflation, with inflation wiping out wage gains for seven straight months, per coverage of the report. Some hiring was tied to AI data center construction and manufacturing (NBC News).

On the Fed, traders raised the odds of a quarter-point hike at the Dec. 8-9 meeting to about 77% on CME FedWatch, coverage of the report said, but Axios reported a rate hike 'isn't a sure thing' and bond markets treated the data as no major shift. Oxford Economics noted falling tech stocks and oil could remove the case for more hikes in 2027.
Gold fell about 1% as the payrolls lifted the dollar and yields, CNBC reported.
facts: Payrolls rose 165,000 in October (CNBC, Fox Business).
Unemployment fell to 4.1% (CNBC).
Average hourly earnings rose 3.1% from a year earlier (Fox Business).
CME FedWatch odds of a December hike rose to about 77% (CNBC and Axios coverage).
The Fed meets Dec. 8-9.
stories.left: Hiring is better, but workers are still losing ground when wages lag prices. Democrats say affordability, not jobs, drove the election, and that tariffs and the war keep costs high. They note that low turnover and part-time work show strain behind the headline.
stories.right: The Washington Examiner says the labor market is strong despite voter discontent and credits the administration's policies. Conservatives argue that a rate hike signals an overheating economy rather than weakness. Some caution that high rates and AI debt pressures could still slow growth.
stories.next: The Fed meets Dec. 8-9; the next jobs report comes in early December.

stories.title: Nasdaq rebounds 1.09% after its worst day in 18 months, with chips leading and the Dow lower
stories.summary: Chips recovered from Thursday's rout, but the Nasdaq still sits in a correction as investors weigh AI regulation.
story: The Nasdaq rose 1.09% to 24,579.42 Friday, a partial bounce from Thursday's 5.52% drop, its worst day since April 2025, CNBC and Fox Business reported. The S&P 500 gained 0.31% to 7,376.86 and the Dow fell 0.46% to 51,285.73. The Nasdaq remains more than 10% below its high. Nvidia rose 2.78% to $186.64 and Tesla rose 4.23% to $358.22. CNBC said the semiconductor index rose about 4.2% and Micron and Qualcomm gained more than 5%.

Thursday's rout followed Democratic wins that investors read as a threat to the AI buildout. Nvidia fell 9.26%, losing almost $450 billion in market value, and the Dow fell 1,833 points, CNBC reported. Qualcomm's weak forecast added to the slide. Voters rejected data centers in 40 of 41 local ballot measures, and Texas governor-elect Gina Hinojosa wants a moratorium on new permits (CNBC, Axios).

Analysts disagree about the damage. Barclays called the pushback 'bipartisan but local,' making the buildout pricier rather than stalling it, and Nomura noted most 2027 capacity is already under construction (CNBC). Trump blamed Democrats for the drop (Fox Business). OpenAI's CFO told CNBC the company will keep investing in data centers.
The 10-year Treasury yield was 4.86% and bitcoin about $75,874.
facts: Nasdaq closed at 24,579.42, up 1.09% (live data; CNBC).
Nvidia fell 9.26% Thursday and rose 2.78% Friday (CNBC, Fox Business).
Voters sided against data centers in 40 of 41 local ballot measures (CNBC).
Nvidia reports earnings Nov. 17 after the close.
stories.why: The AI trade is now a political trade as well as a technology bet. Local limits and a possible federal moratorium raise costs for the buildout that supports chip, cloud and power company earnings, and the Fed's possible hike makes the pressure worse.
stories.next: Nvidia reports Nov. 17 after the close; the Fed meets Dec. 8-9.

stories.title: Texas has 474 GW of data center grid requests, more than five times its record peak demand
stories.summary: Abbott paused approvals for an audit, and governor-elect Hinojosa wants a moratorium until lawmakers pass protections.
story: ERCOT is weighing more than 474 gigawatts of grid connection requests, over five times Texas's record peak demand, and about 90% are data centers, according to Gov. Greg Abbott as reported by Axios. A December 2025 figure put the queue at more than 220 GW, so it has more than doubled. Abbott directed regulators to deny connections to projects that fail requirements and later ordered the environmental regulator to pause data center permits pending an audit (CNBC, Axios).

Democrat Gina Hinojosa won the governor's race and has proposed a moratorium until the legislature passes protections on water, electricity, air and property rights, CNBC reported. She takes office in January, and the legislative session ends in mid-2027. Goldman Sachs estimates moratoriums could affect 45% of planned US capacity, and SemiAnalysis says Texas holds 41% of new US capacity in 2028 (CNBC).

The engineering problem goes beyond permits. AI loads swing sharply, and ERCOT's Large Load Working Group is evaluating 800-volt DC designs, IEEE Spectrum reports. Nvidia says 800 VDC reduces copper, because a 1 MW rack could need 200 kg of busbar, and expects such facilities in 2027. IEEE notes standards and safety frameworks are still being developed.
Trump attacked the moratorium and said Texas should change course 'IMMEDIATELY' (CNBC).
stories.flag: The 474 GW figure is Abbott's own claim as reported by Axios; many requests are speculative and will not all be built.
facts: ERCOT is considering more than 474 GW of connection requests (Abbott, via Axios).
About 90% of new requests are data centers (Abbott, via Axios).
Hinojosa's moratorium would last until the legislature passes protections (CNBC).
Goldman estimates moratoriums could affect 45% of planned US capacity (CNBC).
800 VDC facilities are expected to start appearing in 2027 (IEEE Spectrum).
stories.why: Grid capacity, not chips, is now the limit on AI. Texas decisions on permits and on how large loads ride through voltage swings will set the pace for the nation's largest data center market.
stories.next: Hinojosa takes office in January; watch ERCOT's large-load rules and the audit results.

stories.title: Energy Dome's CO2 batteries move toward more grid projects, with efficiency trade-offs
stories.summary: The long-duration storage uses compressed carbon dioxide and is claimed to be cheaper than lithium-ion, though roundtrip efficiency is about 70%.
story: Energy Dome's CO2 battery stores electricity by compressing carbon dioxide, and IEEE Spectrum reports the design is being replicated at several sites in 2026, including a project for Alliant Energy in Wisconsin that has the all-clear to start construction and would power 18,000 homes. MIT Technology Review reports it can deliver power for up to 24 hours.

Cost claims vary by source. IEEE Spectrum cites an expectation that the system will be about 30% cheaper than lithium-ion, while MIT Technology Review says the company estimates 10% to 15% cheaper for an eight-hour system. Technology Review puts roundtrip efficiency at about 70% and notes that only one commercial project is operating so far.

MIT Technology Review also flags that some plants pair the technology with natural gas turbines, a possible climate concern. Separately, it reported US battery installations hit a record 20.2 GWh in the second quarter, on pace for about 71 GWh in 2026.
The case for long-duration storage grows as data centers add large, steady loads that strain grids.
stories.flag: The Wisconsin project's size and timeline come from IEEE Spectrum alone.
facts: The system compresses CO2 to store energy and can deliver up to 24 hours (MIT Technology Review).
Roundtrip efficiency is about 70% (MIT Technology Review).
One commercial project is operating so far (MIT Technology Review).
Cost claims range from 10% to 30% below lithium-ion (MIT Technology Review, IEEE Spectrum).
US battery installs hit a record 20.2 GWh in Q2 2026 (MIT Technology Review).
stories.why: Lithium-ion dominates short storage, but multi-hour and multi-day storage is the weak spot. CO2 batteries use cheap, common equipment and could help utilities integrate solar and wind, if efficiency and cost hold up in real projects.
stories.next: Watch for Alliant's Wisconsin construction start and operating data from the first commercial plant.

stories.title: NASA's Swift telescope re-enters over Indonesia after a failed private rescue
stories.summary: The US Space Force confirmed re-entry Nov. 4 after 22 years and more than 2,000 gamma-ray bursts.
story: NASA's Swift Observatory re-entered Earth's atmosphere on Nov. 4 at 7:39 a.m. EST over the North Sumatra region of Indonesia, the US Space Force confirmed, according to NASA. NASA ended operations Oct. 23 after the last science observation on Oct. 20. NASA expected most of the spacecraft to burn up and put the odds of debris harming anyone at 1 in 2,100.

The rescue failed. NASA paid Katalyst Space Technologies about $30 million for LINK, a refrigerator-sized craft meant to grab Swift with robotic arms and lift its orbit, Space.com reported. LINK launched July 3, then propulsion and reaction wheel problems made it spin unexpectedly. It got within about 12 to 15 km of Swift and photographed it. Science reported NASA abandoned the boost attempt.

Katalyst's CEO said the timeline was the main constraint and that three or even 12 more months would have made a tremendous difference, Space.com reported. Swift had no thrusters to fight atmospheric drag.
Over its career Swift observed more than 2,000 gamma-ray bursts, and its data contributed to about 7,000 papers, NASA says. The archive is public.
facts: Swift re-entered Nov. 4 at 7:39 a.m. EST over North Sumatra (NASA).
NASA paid about $30 million for the rescue attempt (Space.com).
LINK launched July 3 and lost stability in orbit (Space.com).
Swift observed more than 2,000 gamma-ray bursts (NASA).
About 7,000 papers used Swift data (NASA).
stories.why: Swift's loss removes a fast-response gamma-ray burst telescope that alerted other observatories to explosions. The failed rescue shows how hard orbital servicing is and how tight the time window can be.
stories.next: NASA has published lessons learned from the boost mission; watch for follow-up plans for servicing aging telescopes such as Hubble.

stories.title: Hubble finds nearby dwarf galaxies hold far less oxygen than expected
stories.summary: A study of 37 dwarf galaxies suggests supernova-driven winds strip oxygen more effectively than models predict.
story: NASA's Hubble team reported Nov. 2 that 37 nearby dwarf galaxies hold much less oxygen than expected, in a study published in The Astrophysical Journal. Each galaxy is close enough for Hubble to resolve individual stars and has a mass at which theory predicts supernova winds should expel oxygen. The team also used archival Spitzer data and radio observations from the Very Large Array and Australian Telescope Compact Array.

The finding comes from the Galaxies Losing Oxygen via Winds (GLOW) project. A data paper on arXiv describes the project's sample, which spans three decades in stellar mass and uses oxygen to trace the cycle of star formation and chemical enrichment in low-mass galaxies.

Energy from massive stars and supernova-driven winds appears to remove oxygen more effectively than current models predict, NASA says. It is unclear whether the missing oxygen sits in the surrounding gas or has left entirely.
The lead researcher plans to use Hubble to study the massive stars that produce and eject the oxygen.
stories.flag: Coverage found is from NASA and the project's data paper; I did not find independent expert commentary.
facts: The study covers 37 nearby dwarf galaxies (NASA).
It was published in The Astrophysical Journal and announced Nov. 2 (NASA).
It is part of the GLOW project (NASA, arXiv).
Supernova winds appear to remove more oxygen than models predict (NASA).
Whether the oxygen sits nearby or escaped is unknown (NASA).
stories.why: Simulations of galaxy growth depend on how much heavy-element gas winds carry away. If models underestimate that loss, estimates of how galaxies enrich their surroundings need revision.
stories.next: Follow-up Hubble work on individual massive stars is planned; no date is given.

stories.title: Anthropic's revised S-1 shows $17 billion in Q3 revenue and $895.4 billion in purchase commitments
stories.summary: Revenue is surging, but growth slowed to about 47% and the filing shows huge compute commitments and losses.
story: Anthropic's amended S-1, filed around Nov. 2, reports about $17 billion in third-quarter revenue and about $895.4 billion in purchase commitments and leases, substantially all for compute and infrastructure, CNBC, Axios and Bloomberg reported. About $447.5 billion would be incurred by the end of 2030 and nearly $70 billion within 12 months of Sept. 30, per CNBC.

CNBC reports third-quarter growth of about 47%, down from 144% in Q2 and 132% in Q1. Bloomberg said revenue was roughly twelve times the $1.4 billion of a year earlier. CNBC also reports a Q3 net loss of $23.29 billion and a nine-month loss of about $104 billion, most of it from fair-value changes on convertible notes and derivatives. Earlier reports put the first-half operating loss at $693 million.

Investors are split. Bulls point to growth and an 85% gross margin, while critics call the IPO speculative, CNBC reported. Axios noted the FT reported Anthropic may not secure an investment-grade rating on its debt. CNBC also reported that Kalshi odds of an IPO announcement dropped after the midterms and AI selloff.
The deal could set the tone for AI listings if it goes ahead.
stories.flag: Figures come from news reports of the filing; I did not read the S-1 itself. Growth percentages may refer to sequential comparisons.
facts: Q3 revenue was about $17 billion (CNBC, Bloomberg).
Purchase commitments total about $895.4 billion (CNBC, Axios).
Q3 growth was about 47%, down from 144% in Q2 (CNBC).
Net loss was $23.29 billion in Q3, mostly non-cash items (CNBC).
Kalshi odds of an IPO announcement fell after the midterms (CNBC).
stories.why: This is the biggest test of whether public investors will fund AI labs at current compute costs. A weak AI stock market raises the price of that capital.
stories.next: Watch for an IPO date or pricing range, and for the next S-1 amendment.

stories.title: Sanders and House Democrats call for a national data center moratorium as Republicans split
stories.summary: Many Republicans favor local limits but reject a federal ban, and Trump rejects slowing the buildout.
story: Sen. Bernie Sanders posted 'National data center moratorium now' after the midterms, CNBC reported. Rep. Yassamin Ansari said pausing AI development should be a top priority on Day 1, Rep. Frank Pallone favors a moratorium until data centers are shown not to harm air, water and power bills, and Rep. Ro Khanna's proposed Data Center Bill of Rights would ban data centers within 2,500 feet of homes and schools.

Republicans are divided. Sen. Jon Husted said the decision should be local, and Michigan Senate nominee Mike Rogers backs a moratorium but opposes a federal ban, Fox News reported. A Gallup poll cited by Fox found 70% of Americans do not want new AI data centers in their towns. The Washington Examiner's opinion section argued House Republicans validate the left's moratorium push and risk US dominance over China.

Trump has rejected calls to slow development. Axios called the election 'an AI earthquake,' with voters rejecting data centers in 40 of 41 local ballot measures. OpenAI's CFO told CNBC the company will keep investing regardless.
Several of the Republican quotes date to before the election.
stories.flag: Some Republican statements come from September coverage, not after the election, and the Washington Examiner pieces are opinion.
facts: Sanders called for a national data center moratorium (CNBC).
Voters rejected data centers in 40 of 41 local measures (CNBC, Axios).
A Gallup poll found 70% oppose new local AI data centers (Fox News).
Many Republicans back local, not federal, limits (Fox News).
Trump has rejected slowing AI development (Fox News).
stories.left: Residents bear higher power bills, water use and noise while tech companies capture the gains. Progressives say a pause until protections exist is common sense. They argue voters in both parties have shown they want a say.
stories.right: A federal ban would cede AI leadership to China and raise costs for consumers and businesses. Conservatives say communities should decide locally through zoning and utility rules, and that a federal moratorium gives Washington power over every project. Some Republicans, though, back state limits.
stories.why: Data center policy now decides how fast US AI capacity can grow. It affects chips, power and the valuations of AI companies.
stories.next: Democrats take the House Jan. 3; the first moratorium bills and hearings are likely in 2027.

briefs: California's Prop 40 billionaire tax appears headed for defeat, trailing about 55.6% to 44.4% with 60% counted, while competing Prop 42 led, CalMatters reported.
CoreWeave's 2032 bond yield topped 16% and its five-year credit default swaps rose above 1,289 basis points, CNBC reported, while Goldman and Janus Henderson call the move overdone.
OpenAI released a cybersecurity model to its top Daybreak Red tier, and Axios reports it found ways to attack nearly 1,000 Linux flaws, while TechCrunch asks whether the access is enough.
Alameda County supervisors want answers from Alameda Health System after ICE brought a detainee to Highland Hospital, KQED reported.
Quanta Magazine revisits experiments in which researchers inject concepts into AI models and find they notice about 20% of the time, and notes researchers dispute whether that is introspection.
Gold fell about 1% after the payrolls report lifted the dollar and yields, CNBC reported.
